title: The Mirror — From One Person to a Society
subtitle: Welfarism, Pareto, the industrialisation paradox

lines.text: A government planner surveys residents about a proposed education and skills centre.
What will we do with it? We need work now.
Our children should study, but fees and transport are the problem.
We're managing. Why spend money on something people may not use?
The planner concludes: the community does not want further education. The centre is cancelled. The budget is redirected.
The community's preferences have been respected. But those preferences may have formed under the same pressures we watched in Aarav's life — scaled to thousands of people.
When an entire community has adapted to deprivation, aggregating their preferences does not escape the problem. It magnifies it.
This is where Sen's critique of utilitarian evaluation becomes structural. Traditional utilitarian social choice rests on three pillars:
Welfarism — evaluate a society through people's reported utility.
Sum-ranking — add those utilities together.
Consequentialism — judge a policy by the state of affairs it produces.

If preferences have adapted to deprivation, welfarism records that adaptation as satisfaction. Sum-ranking aggregates it. Consequentialism calls the outcome acceptable. The framework is internally consistent — and blind to the process that produced the numbers.

A related concept: Pareto optimality — a state in which no one can be made better off without making someone worse off. A neighbourhood can be Pareto optimal and deeply unjust at the same time. Optimality is an efficiency criterion, not a moral verdict.
Consider a harder case. Before industrialisation, a community's wants are modest and mostly met. People report contentment.
Then industry arrives — new jobs, new goods, new horizons — but also new inequality, new disruption, new aspirations that cannot yet be fulfilled.
Reported satisfaction may fall even as real possibilities expand.
Should we preserve the earlier state because people were happier? Or accept the frustrations of transition because the world has opened up?
A policy that preserves low aspirations because they produce high satisfaction risks making adaptation into a reason to never change anything.
But a policy that imposes change because outsiders think they know better risks destroying autonomy in the name of freedom.
There is no clean exit from this dilemma. There is only the obligation to see it clearly — and to ensure that when opportunities expand, people have a genuine say in what happens next.
